title: Former Cal softball player files suit alleging ex-coach pressured her into a relationship
content:
A former University of California, Berkeley softball player is suing the school and former head softball coach Chelsea Spencer, alleging that the coach pressured her into a sexual relationship and reduced her playing opportunities when she tried to distance herself.

The player, who is referred to as Jane Doe in the lawsuit, filed the complaint Aug. 24 in Alameda County (Calif.) Superior Court. The complaint names Spencer, the University of California’s Board of Regents, unidentified people including “administrators, athletic directors, supervisors, employees, agents” and other individuals who “participated in, facilitated, enabled, concealed, ratified, or are otherwise responsible for the intentional misconduct.”

The filing, obtained by The Athletic, accuses Spencer of sexual assault and battery and intentional infliction of emotional distress. It also accuses the university of negligence on multiple fronts, alleging that Cal’s own investigation found Spencer violated campus policy on conflicts of interest in consensual relationships. The former player is seeking a jury trial and unspecified damages.

A Cal spokesperson declined to comment on the lawsuit and the investigation.

Michael Carney, a managing partner at Slater Slater Schulman, the law firm representing the plaintiff, told The Athletic: “Our client came to UC Berkeley to pursue her lifelong dream of playing softball at the highest level, in an environment where she could focus on her sport and her education. Instead, she was placed in an impossible position by a coach who held power over her future and by a university that failed to enforce its own policies.”

Carney added: “No student-athlete should have to choose between resisting exploitation and protecting the career she worked her whole life to build. We look forward to holding UC Berkeley and coach Spencer accountable.”

According to the lawsuit, Spencer allegedly began communicating with the player “outside the ordinary confines of a coach-athlete relationship” around September 2023, calling and texting her every day and sending direct messages on social media, which eventually became romantic. Spencer allegedly told the former player, “you’re so beautiful” and “your girlfriend is so lucky.” Spencer also allegedly gave the player “special attention and privileges,” such as money and gifts. The lawsuit alleges Spencer threatened self-harm when the player discussed ending the relationship.

According to the filing, as Spencer’s communications increased, the player was expected to “remain readily available” throughout the day. When the player did not answer Spencer’s messages, the coach grew angry and reduced the player’s playing time, the complaint alleges.

“When (the player) did not provide Spencer the attention she demanded, Spencer yelled at (her), treated her differently, and reduced or withheld playing opportunities,” the filing says. “(The player) began to recognize, even before the relationship became sexual, that Spencer’s personal demands and Spencer’s authority as head coach were intertwined.”

The relationship became sexual during a softball trip in May 2024, according to the lawsuit, when Spencer invited the player to her hotel room. The sexual contact continued for a year, according to the filing. The filing also says Spencer brought up suicide “to prevent (the player) from withdrawing,” and when the player discussed ending the relationship, Spencer allegedly threatened to kill herself.

The player also alleges that multiple members of the coaching staff, including Spencer’s wife at the time, “knew of, observed, or received information” about Spencer’s relationship with the player. The filing says that “no effective action was taken” by the staff to separate Spencer from the player.

The complaint also states that in February 2025, other softball players reported concerns about Spencer’s relationship with the player to associate athletic director Gordon Bayne and that Spencer was giving the player “special privileges and preferential treatment because of the relationship.”

In May 2025, according to the complaint, Spencer spoke with Bayne about her relationship with the player, and the player allegedly was removed from the program and did not compete in her senior season. Bayne remains employed at Cal.

Spencer, a Cal alumna, stepped down as head coach in June 2025, deciding to “prioritize my mental health and my family.” She led the Golden Bears to NCAA Tournament appearances in the final three of her five years at the school and had signed a three-year contract extension in February 2025.
